beats.headline: Stop writing 500-line service methods.
beats.subline: If-else chains are a maintenance nightmare. Strategy patterns turn logic into interchangeable components.
beats.narration: If your service methods are drowning in if-else chains checking status enums, your code is rigid. Let's replace that sprawl with the Strategy pattern.

beats.title: Branching vs. Strategy
beats.narration: Hard-coded branches force you to edit working code every time a new carrier arrives. Strategy encapsulates those rules, letting you swap algorithms at runtime.

beats.title: Functional Strategy

steps.explanation: Allows passing logic as a lambda, removing the need for verbose concrete classes.
Clean, stateless logic that is easy to test and maintain.

beats.narration: In modern Java, you don't need a class for every rule. Use a functional interface and pass lambdas directly for stateless formulas.

beats.title: Strategy Lookup Map

nodes.label: List<Strategy>
nodes.detail: Injected list of all available implementations

nodes.label: Map<String, Strategy>
nodes.detail: Unmodifiable map keyed by carrier code

beats.narration: For complex stateful strategies, use a lookup map. Inject all implementations, map them by key, and call them without a single branch.

beats.title: Strategy Locked In
takeaways: Use lookup maps for DI-managed beans
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Fixing the Lapsed Listener memory leak →
beats.narration: Strategy keeps your services lean. In Part 2, we tackle the Observer pattern and the silent memory leaks that kill long-running JVMs.

beats.headline: Your event listeners are leaking memory.
beats.subline: The Lapsed Listener Problem is a silent killer in long-running Java apps.
beats.narration: Think your event system is solid? If your publisher holds strong references to short-lived listeners, you've got a memory leak waiting to happen.

beats.title: The Lapsed Listener Fix

steps.explanation: Forces callers to acknowledge the lifecycle of the subscription.
Returns a handle that removes the listener, preventing the leak.

beats.narration: Never let listeners subscribe without a way to unsubscribe. Return an AutoCloseable handle so callers can clean up in a try-with-resources block.

beats.title: Safe Event Broadcast
beats.narration: Use CopyOnWriteArrayList to keep iteration thread-safe. Wrap every listener call in a try-catch so one broken subscriber doesn't crash your entire event chain.

beats.title: Lifecycle Management
beats.caption: Deterministic unsubscription
beats.narration: By using try-with-resources, the listener is removed the moment the block exits. No more dangling references, no more heap bloat.

beats.title: Observer Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): The Command Pattern & Undo logic →
beats.narration: Observer is now leak-proof. In Part 3, we turn actions into objects with the Command pattern, enabling undo-stacks and transaction logs.

beats.headline: Turn your operations into objects.
beats.subline: Commands let you queue, log, and undo actions with ease.
beats.narration: When an action needs more than just execution—like undo history or audit logs—it's time to graduate from simple Runnables to the Command pattern.

beats.title: Command with Undo

steps.explanation: Defines the action and its inverse operation.
Captures all context needed to perform or reverse the action.

beats.narration: A Command object encapsulates the receiver and the parameters. By storing the state, you can easily implement an undo stack for your transactions.

beats.title: Invoker & History
beats.narration: The invoker tracks history. When a rollback is requested, it pops the last command and calls undo. It's clean, decoupled, and highly testable.

beats.title: Runnable vs. Command
beats.narration: Don't over-engineer. Use Runnables for simple tasks. Use full Command objects only when you need state, undo, or auditability.

beats.title: Command Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Java 21 Sealed State Machines →
beats.narration: Command patterns make your system reversible. In Part 4, we use Java 21's sealed interfaces to build bulletproof state machines.

beats.headline: Stop checking nulls for state transitions.
beats.subline: Java 21 sealed interfaces make state machines type-safe and exhaustive.
beats.narration: State machines used to be a mess of enums and null checks. With Java 21, we can use sealed interfaces to make illegal states unrepresentable.

beats.title: Sealed State Machine

steps.explanation: Explicitly defines allowed states, preventing unexpected extensions.
Holds only the data relevant to that specific state.

beats.narration: Records are perfect for states. A 'Paid' state holds a transaction ID, while 'Created' doesn't. No more null fields for data that doesn't exist yet.

beats.title: Exhaustive Switch

steps.explanation: Compiler ensures all states are handled.
Adding a new state triggers a compiler error if not handled.

beats.narration: The compiler now forces you to handle every state. If you add a 'Delivered' state, the code won't compile until you update your transitions.

beats.title: State Transition
beats.narration: This is type-safe state management. You can't pay for an already paid order, and the compiler guarantees you haven't missed any edge cases.

beats.title: State Locked In
beats.narration: Sealed state machines are the gold standard for lifecycle logic. In Part 5, we wrap up with Template Method and avoiding inheritance pitfalls.

beats.headline: Don't let subclasses break your workflow.
beats.subline: Template Method enforces the skeleton, while hooks allow customization.
beats.narration: Need a fixed workflow but flexible steps? Template Method keeps the skeleton final, ensuring no one skips your critical audit or auth steps.

beats.title: Template Method

steps.explanation: The workflow skeleton is locked. Subclasses cannot reorder steps.
Hooks allow customization of specific steps.

beats.narration: The final method defines the sequence. Subclasses only implement the abstract hooks, keeping the overall pipeline logic safe and predictable.

beats.title: Template vs. Composition
beats.narration: Inheritance is rigid. If you don't need shared protected state, prefer composition with functional interfaces. It's easier to test and reuse.

beats.title: The Constructor Trap
beats.caption: Avoid this common mistake
beats.narration: Never call overridable methods from a constructor. Subclass fields aren't initialized yet, leading to nasty NullPointerExceptions.

beats.title: Patterns Mastered
takeaways: Never call abstract methods in constructors
beats.narration: You've mastered behavioral patterns. Checkout the branch, run the lab, and start refactoring those if-else chains into clean, testable code.
